The first two days were the loudest. Not outside, where it was mostly birdsong and the particular hush of a place with no traffic, but inside, where my own thoughts kept arriving at full volume, uninvited, cataloguing everything I was supposedly missing back home.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

By day four, meals had stopped being something you talked through. You sat, you ate, you noticed the sound of your own chewing in a way that felt slightly absurd the first time and then just felt normal. Nobody was performing being fine. Nobody was asking how you were doing in that automatic way people ask without wanting the real answer.

There was a lot of silence, a lot of walking between sessions with nothing to say, and a version of my own thoughts that got progressively harder to keep up with, because there was less and less feeding them.

I went into a weeklong personal-development retreat that leaned heavily on Vipassana-style silent meditation, and I went in openly skeptical. I have spent enough of my adult life reading psychology research to be wary of anything marketed as transformation in a fixed number of days. What I did not expect was how much of the shift had nothing to do with any specific technique and everything to do with simply being somewhere else, on a schedule that had gone quiet on purpose.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The narrator that would not stop, and then did

The part of the mind that runs constant self-commentary, replaying conversations, rehearsing ones that have not happened yet, narrating your own day back to you as you live it, is not a metaphor. It corresponds to an actual, well-mapped set of brain regions called the default mode network, active precisely when you are not focused on an external task, and unusually busy in people who ruminate. Quieting it has historically been hard to do on demand. It is the reason a walk in nature or a good conversation can feel like relief in a way that is difficult to name: something in you that had been running nonstop finally idles.

A study published in November 2025 in the journal [*Communications Biology*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-025-09088-3) put that idling under an fMRI scanner. Researchers scanned twenty adults, selected from a much larger group of retreat participants, before and after a seven-day residential program in San Diego that combined lectures, guided meditation and group practices, no substances involved at any point. After the week, default mode network connectivity had dropped sharply and significantly, and participants’ scores on a standard measure of mystical or ego-dissolving experience rose to a level the study’s lead researcher [described as comparable](https://neurosciencenews.com/meditation-brain-immune-system-29905/) to what typically requires *psilocybin*.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Nobody in the room had taken anything.

The brain had gotten there on its own, apparently, given a week with almost nothing else competing for its attention.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

I want to be careful with that finding, because it is easy to overstate. It is one observational study, with no separate control group who spent a week doing something else entirely, so it cannot tell us how much of the change came from the meditation specifically versus the retreat format in general, the isolation, the routine, the simple absence of a phone. I am a researcher, not a clinician, and I do not think a single imaging study is grounds for anyone to treat a retreat as medical treatment for anything, or as a substitute for actual mental health care if what someone needs is more than a quieter week. What I do think it offers is a real, physiological reason for something a lot of people already report anecdotally: that the quiet gets loud in a different way after a few days, and then, without much warning, it does not.

Rumination, the specific, repetitive, self-focused replaying that the default mode network seems to specialize in, has its own research history separate from this single study, and most of it points the same direction: chronic overactivity in that network correlates with anxiety and depressive symptoms, and interventions that reliably interrupt it, whether meditation, absorbing physical activity, or simply a sustained change of environment, tend to track with people reporting more relief than the specific technique alone would predict.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[A 2025 University of Toronto study found that actively trying to make yourself happier can paradoxically undermine the very behaviours that create happiness — because the effort of constantly regulating how you feel appears to drain the same limited mental resources used for persistence, self-control and resisting temptation.](https://theartfulage.com/t-happiness-pursuit-self-control-persistence-temptation/?utm_source=spacedaily.com&utm_campaign=editorial&utm_medium=editorial_pick&utm_content=t-happiness-pursuit-self-control-persistence-temptation)

That is part of why I am wary of crediting any one method too heavily. The nervous system does not seem to care much which door you used to get quiet. It mostly seems to care that you actually got there, and stayed long enough for it to register.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## What I used to assume retreats were selling

My skepticism was never really about whether people felt better afterward. Plenty of things make people feel better temporarily, a vacation, a good meal, a few days without email. What I doubted was the story retreats tend to tell about themselves, that a particular breathing technique or a specific ritual is doing something uniquely powerful that ordinary life cannot replicate. I still think a lot of that framing oversells the method and undersells the plainer explanation.

The plainer explanation, at least from where I sat for a week, is unglamorous. Changing location does something on its own, before any technique gets applied to it, simply by removing the physical cues that keep your usual patterns running. Silence removes another layer, the constant low-grade performance of being okay for other people. And having actual, unhurried time to think, real hours with nothing scheduled into them, seems to matter more than any single practice performed inside those hours. I am not entirely sure meditation itself was the active ingredient so much as it was the container that made the other three things possible at the same volume, for that long, without interruption.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Still figuring out what any of it means

I would not describe myself as converted, exactly. I think I have moved from dismissing retreats outright to something closer to: maybe they work, for some people, some of the time, if you actually let them, rather than spending the week half-performing participation while mentally drafting the article you plan to write about it afterward, which I will admit I caught myself doing more than once.

What stayed with me longer than any single session was smaller than a breakthrough. It was noticing, on day six or seven, that the version of myself narrating my own life back to me had gone quiet enough that I could hear other things instead, footsteps, birds, a kettle, my own breathing.

Whether that is psilocybin-adjacent neuroscience or just what happens to any brain given a week without its usual inputs, I genuinely do not know yet. I am still figuring out what part of it was the place, what part was the silence, and what part was simply having permission, for seven days, to stop narrating and just be somewhere.
